job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Gareth Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I finished a finance degree at Ashby College in the summer, and I'm back in my old room at my parents' house in Corlin, a small town with one main street. I get up at eight, read the job listings in the local paper and on two websites, and write out applications by hand first before I type them. In the afternoon I help my dad, who's a land surveyor, file his paperwork, and on weekends I work my allotment.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of all that, and what part do you still like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hardest part is that I'm not a fast mover, and the whole thing moves fast. I've applied for about forty jobs and had two phone calls. What I still like is careful, orderly work: during my internship at the Corlin Savings branch I checked loan files for a month, and I liked finding the one missing signature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's about what I expected. A lot of the fuss was people selling something. I'd tell my dad that the market does what the market does, and we'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change my problem. I have a degree, some student debt and about two months saved, and I still don't have an offer. The routine tasks AI takes over might include the loan-file checking I did, but only a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now: forty or so applications, a phone call to every firm after a week, and I'd visit the Corlin Savings manager again in person. I'd keep helping my dad for pocket money. I wouldn't start using any AI tools, because I don't see why I should trust them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady but a bit heavy. I'm not frightened, I'm just tired of explaining to relatives at Sunday lunch why I haven't got a job yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a fast mover. Does that help or hurt you in a job search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow helps me with accuracy, so I get praised for it in an internship. But in a job search it hurts, because firms want a quick answer, a lively email and a person who is already comfortable with every system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the search went on another six months, what would be the first thing to give?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The allotment and the weekend trips would go first. Not because they cost much, but because I'd feel guilty spending anything on myself while my parents still feed me.

say: I'd say it's **about what I expected**, because a lot of the fuss was people selling something.
I'd tell my dad the market does what it does, so we **wait and see**.
think: AI hype or not, I still have **debt and no offer**, and the loan-file checking might shrink a little.
I'm tired of **explaining to relatives** why I have no job yet.
do: Send **about forty applications** and phone each firm a week later.
Visit the **Corlin Savings manager** in person and keep filing paperwork for my dad.
Stay away from **AI tools** because I don't trust them.
feel: It feels **steady but heavy**, and mostly embarrassing at Sunday lunch.
S0.quote: I'm not frightened, I'm just tired of explaining to relatives at Sunday lunch why I haven't got a job yet.
fieldNote: Gareth's worry is **practical and personal**: no offer, debt and family pressure, not technology.
He prefers **in-person routes** like visiting the bank manager, which suits his slow style.
He feels **guilt about spending** while his parents support him.

steps.text: Send forty job applications and phone each firm after a week
Visit the Corlin Savings branch manager in person
Help my dad file his surveying paperwork for pocket money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should wait and see what actually changes, because everyone predicts things. But I'd also say banks shouldn't use it as an excuse to cut the few entry jobs that exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my kind of job is exactly the one on the card. Checking files, matching figures and answering customer questions are what a graduate in a bank does, and a program can do those in a blink. I'm worried there won't be an entry rung left by the time I'm ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same search but add a few jobs where a person must be present, like branch banking, a local building society or an accountancy in a market town. I'd ask the bank manager about any training scheme. I'd also pay for one evening course in a basic spreadsheet program, because I know I'm behind on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels uncomfortable, like the ground tilting slowly. Nothing dramatic, but I notice it on the edge of every conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your internship at the bank do you think software could take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The file checking and the figure matching would go first. What stays is the part where a customer sits across a desk and wants someone to explain, and the part where someone has to sign a form and be held responsible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take for you to try one of these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my dad's friend at the building society showed me, in the office, on a real file, I'd try it. I need to see it done by somebody I trust, not a video from a stranger.

say: I'd say **we should wait and** see what really changes, because everyone predicts things.
I'd say banks shouldn't use AI as an **excuse** to cut the few entry jobs.
think: The card describes **exactly my job**: checking files, matching figures and answering customers.
I worry **no entry rung** is left by the time I'm ready.
do: Add **branch banking and building** societies in market towns to my search.
Ask the bank manager about **training schemes** that put a person at a desk.
Pay for **one evening course** in spreadsheets, because I know I'm behind.
feel: It feels **uncomfortable**, like the ground tilting slowly.
S1.quote: I need to see it done by somebody I trust, not a video from a stranger.
fieldNote: Gareth's resistance is **not stubbornness**; he'd try tools if a trusted person showed him in person.
He expects the **entry rung** of banking to shrink first and says so plainly.
His public line is **cautious**, while his private worry is sharper.

steps.text: Apply to branch banks and building societies in market towns
Ask the bank manager about training schemes
Pay for an evening spreadsheet course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and think, because two years isn't enough for anyone. I'd want governments and the banks to say clearly what they are going to do, instead of leaving families to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel finished before I started. If AI does desk work as well as a person and cheaper, then my degree is worth a lot less, and nobody is going to wait for a slow learner like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents the first week and agree a budget for living at home for as long as needed. I'd look at work where people are still needed, perhaps my dad's surveying firm or the garden centre, since robots are three years behind. And I'd put all my savings into an account that's safe, not shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long dark corridor. I'd lie awake doing sums, which I'm good at, but the sums don't come out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, who would you lean on, and for what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on my parents first, and on my dad's friends in the town, since they know who's hiring. Not on the government, though I'd probably have to ask it for something anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents, and in what words?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, 'Dad, I might be living here a long time, and I'd like us to plan for it together.' I'd rather say it early and plainly than let them guess.

say: I'd say we need to **slow down**, because two years isn't enough for anyone.
I'd want governments and banks to **say clearly** what they will do.
think: I'd feel **finished before I started**, since desk work would be done better and cheaper.
Nobody will **wait for a slow** learner like me.
do: Agree a **living-at-home budget** with my parents in the first week.
Look at **work that needs people**, like my dad's surveying firm or the garden centre.
Move my savings into a **safe account**, not shares.
feel: It feels like a **long dark corridor**, and I'd lie awake doing sums that don't come out.
S2.quote: If AI does desk work as well as a person and cheaper, then my degree is worth a lot less
fieldNote: Gareth expects to **lose the whole route** into finance, so his mood rises to alarmed.
He turns to **family and local contacts**, not the state, though he admits he may need to ask it.
His **plain, early talk** with his father is a notable detail.

steps.text: Agree a living-at-home budget with my parents
Apply to my dad's surveying firm and the garden centre
Move savings into a safe account
Cut every spending item except food and phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to prepare if banks and colleges start now. I'd say it quietly, though, because I'm not the kind to shout it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still worried. I can see my job could be taken by 2031, but five years gives me the chance to get a first job, pay my debt and learn at least the basics of the new systems. If I'm slow, I'd still be inside the building when it changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any entry role in a bank or accountancy and stay there, learn the systems one at a time, and ask the colleague who sits near me to show me tools. I'd pay down the student debt before anything else. I'd also keep my allotment, because growing vegetables is a good hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a slow weather front. I don't feel panic, but there's a heaviness whenever the news mentions it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me get a foothold before the thinking work disappears. Two years doesn't, because I'd still be applying when it landed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had a job by next spring, what would you do with your first pay cheques?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half to my student loan, a bit to my mum, and the rest in a savings account. I'd keep my spending very dull on purpose for those five years.

say: I'd say **five years is enough** to prepare if banks and colleges start now.
I'd say it quietly, since I'm **not one to shout** online.
think: I can see my job taken by 2031, but five years lets me **get inside the building** first.
I worry I'm **slow to learn** the new systems.
do: Take **any entry role** in a bank or accountancy and learn the systems one at a time.
Pay **down the student debt** before spending on anything else.
Keep my **allotment**, since growing vegetables is a good hedge.
feel: It feels like a **slow weather front**, with a heaviness whenever the news mentions it.
S3.quote: Five years lets me get a foothold before the thinking work disappears.
fieldNote: Gareth sees the **foothold** as the key gain: being inside an employer when change arrives.
He stays at alarmed because he still has **no offer and no** income today.
His response to more time is **steady debt repayment**, not retraining.

steps.text: Take the first entry role in a bank or accountancy
Pay down student debt before anything else
Ask a colleague to show me one tool at a time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and that most predictions in my lifetime have been wrong. I'd say we should keep an eye on it, and I wouldn't change my plans much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd manage. Ten years is long enough to get a first job, pay off the loan, maybe buy a small house in Corlin and still be in work when it arrives. I'd worry about the last few years only.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'm doing: a first job, steady saving, and each year I'd learn a little more about the tools. Maybe by year four I'd take an evening course on the software banks use. I'd stay in Corlin and keep close to my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels distant and a little unreal. I don't think I'd lose any sleep over it until about 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still go for a career in finance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still go for finance, since I like the order of it, but I'd steer towards advice jobs, like helping families with pensions and loans, where people want a face to talk to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be settled by the end of ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the loan gone, a house I own or at least a mortgage I can pay, and my parents comfortable in their old age. If those things are settled, I can handle the rest.

say: I'd say **most predictions** in my lifetime have been wrong, so I wouldn't change plans much.
I'd say we should **keep an eye** on it.
think: Ten years is long enough to **get a job**, clear the loan and own a small house.
I'd only worry about the **last few years**.
do: Get a **first job** and save steadily, learning a little more about the tools each year.
Take an **evening course** on bank software around year four.
Stay in **Corlin** near my parents and steer towards family advice work.
feel: It feels **distant and a little** unreal, nothing I'd lose sleep over until about 2033.
S4.quote: I'd want the loan gone, a house I own or at least a mortgage I can pay, and my parents comfortable in their old age.
fieldNote: Gareth's anxiety falls a notch with a decade, but the **jobless present** keeps it from calm.
His goals are **ordinary and domestic**: loan gone, house, parents looked after.
He plans to move towards **advice work**, where a face still matters.

steps.text: Get a first job and save steadily
Take an evening course on bank software around year four
Steer towards pensions and loan advice for families

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture, without a doubt. I move slowly, and two years is hardly enough to get my first job, let alone adapt. What would help is clear dates and plans from banks and the government, and a training place that takes slow learners seriously.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Perhaps only that slow people aren't stupid, we're careful, and careful is what a bank used to want. I hope that's still worth something.

headlineQuote: Slow people aren't stupid, we're careful, and careful is what a bank used to want.
portrait: Gareth is a 23-year-old **finance graduate** living at his parents' in Corlin, with about forty applications sent and no offer yet.
He has some student debt and **two months of savings**, and he never uses AI tools.
He is pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, blames no one in particular, and trusts **in-person help** from people he knows.
His mood runs from anxious to alarmed at short horizons, because he is **slow to adapt**.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, as he moves slowly and two years is barely enough to get a first job.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear dates and plans** from banks and government, and training places that take slow learners seriously, would help.
